A sole proprietorship is one of the simplest forms of business ownership. It is owned and operated by a single individual, with fewer formalities and relatively simple compliance requirements. This guide covers the key aspects of setting up a sole proprietorship, along with its advantages and limitations.

A sole proprietorship is a business owned and managed by one individual. The proprietor is personally responsible for the business’s debts and liabilities. Unlike a company or LLP, it does not have a separate legal identity from its owner. In India, there is no single central registration for a sole proprietorship; applicable registrations depend on the nature and location of the business.
Steps to Register a Sole Proprietorship
Select a suitable business name and ensure it complies with applicable legal and trademark requirements.
Depending on the business activity and location, registrations such as Shop and Establishment registration, trade licences, or industry-specific permits may be required.
GST registration may be required based on turnover, business activities, and applicable GST provisions.
The proprietor generally uses their individual PAN for income-tax purposes and must comply with applicable tax requirements.
Maintaining a separate account for business transactions helps keep income and expenses organised.
Keep proper records of income, expenses, invoices, and other transactions, along with applicable tax and statutory filings.
Renew applicable licences and comply with tax, labour, municipal, and industry-specific regulations.
Fewer formalities and relatively low setup costs.
The proprietor has complete control over business decisions.
Business income is generally reported as the proprietor’s individual income, subject to applicable tax laws.
The business can be managed or discontinued with comparatively fewer formalities.
The proprietor is personally responsible for business debts and liabilities.
Raising external capital can be more difficult than for companies and other business structures.
The business and proprietor are legally connected, which may affect certain growth and investment opportunities.
